title: Large zero rectangles in low-rank real matrices
area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) of rank \(r\) with at least \(n^2/2\) zero entries, there are nonempty sets \(I,J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\) satisfying \[A_{ij}=0\quad(i\in I,\ j\in J),\qquad |I|\,|J|\ge n^2\exp(-C\sqrt r)?\]
why: The question asks whether low real rank forces a large exact combinatorial pattern when zeros are dense. This connects linear-algebraic complexity to the rectangles that control communication protocols, while extending beyond Boolean matrices. Its value is the proposed general structural principle; the question is not merely to speed up a search for a rectangle.
status_note: Checked on 14 September 2026. The original target is explicit in the 2013 source. The 2024 primary paper and 2025 Oberwolfach report retain the broader real-matrix conjecture; the checked positive results have additional restrictions. No proof or refutation of this precise half-density area bound was located in the bounded search. Cited proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Lovett poses the half-zero-density real-matrix rectangle conjecture and records optimality of the proposed exponent.
Hunter and coauthors prove zero-submatrix bounds under nonnegative-entry and average-entry restrictions, and a related set-system result; their Conjecture 1.8 retains arbitrary real matrices.
Sudakov’s Oberwolfach report continues to state the sparse-real-matrix question as Conjecture 5.

sentences: The question concerns square real matrices with low rank and at least half their entries equal to zero.
It asks for a Cartesian block consisting entirely of zeros whose area is a square-root-exponential fraction of the whole matrix.
The constant in that guarantee must be the same for every matrix and dimension.
The rank is over the real numbers, and entries may have arbitrary signs and magnitudes.
Recent results establish related guarantees under additional entry restrictions, while the checked sources retain the general real-matrix question.

definitions: The rank is the dimension over \(\mathbb R\) of the span of the columns. A zero entry means exact equality to zero. Apart from the zero-density condition, entries may be arbitrary real numbers of either sign and magnitude; there is no finite-alphabet or integrality assumption. A rectangle is a Cartesian product \(I\times J\) of row and column index sets, and its size is its number of entries \(|I||J|\). The sets need not be consecutive, equal, or of the same cardinality. This is an area guarantee, with no separate lower bound prescribed for each side. The exponential is the real exponential function and \(\sqrt r\) is the nonnegative square root. The same constant must work for all dimensions, ranks, entries and zero patterns. When \(r=0\), the entire matrix is zero and the displayed bound asks for the whole matrix. The target is an existence theorem about matrices, not an algorithm with a specified input representation or running time.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal statement, or of its negation. A negative answer must establish that for every real \(C>0\) there exist \(n\ge1\) and an admissible real matrix of rank \(r\) such that every all-zero rectangle has area strictly below \(n^2\exp(-C\sqrt r)\). One finite example violating a chosen constant does not refute the conjecture. A result restricted to Boolean, nonnegative integer, bounded-entry or intersection matrices does not settle the stated arbitrary-real target. No numerical approximation of matrix entries or of a zero test substitutes for exact equality.

context_blocks.text: A matrix can have many zero entries without those entries forming a large Cartesian block. The question asks whether a small dimension of the column span forces such a block, and specifies how much of the matrix it must occupy.

The conjectured area fraction is \(\exp(-C\sqrt r)\). It depends only on rank, even when the number of rows and columns is much larger. The constant is uniform: allowing it to depend on the particular matrix would remove the quantitative content of the question.

Lovett posed this precise half-zero-density, real-matrix, rectangle-area version in the 2013 Dagstuhl report. That report also states that the square-root dependence in the exponent would be best possible. The present formulation keeps its area target rather than requiring a balanced square.

For Boolean communication matrices, a constant rectangle is a collection of input pairs on which the answer is fixed. Low-rank real matrices allow a much wider range of entry values, so a theorem for Boolean matrices alone does not cover this question.

Hunter, Milojević, Sudakov and Tomon retain a broader sparse-real-matrix conjecture as Conjecture 1.8: when at most an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of entries are nonzero, a zero square of side \(n\exp(-O(\sqrt{\varepsilon r}))\) is predicted. That additional density parameter and square-side target are useful context, not replacements for the fixed-density area statement here.

Their Theorem 1.12 proves a related bound for nonnegative matrices whose nonzero entries are at least one and whose average entry is at most one half. In particular it gives the desired rank dependence for Boolean matrices with at least half their entries zero. A density of zeros does not impose the required average-entry bound on an arbitrary real matrix, and arbitrary signed entries fall outside the theorem.

Their Theorem 1.10 also resolves a related cross-disjoint-set-family conjecture, with its exponent measured by the size of the ground set. This result does not identify the ground-set size with the real rank of every matrix. Sudakov’s 2025 Oberwolfach report continues to list the general sparse-real-matrix statement as Conjecture 5.
